response.title: Will a robot mower without a boundary wire work in a yard with lots of big trees, or will it lose its signal and get stuck?
response.answer:
Yes, a robot mower without a boundary wire can work in a yard with lots of big trees—but the navigation technology matters enormously.

If your yard has many large, mature trees with dense canopies, I would be cautious about buying a mower that relies exclusively on GPS/RTK navigation.

The good news is that newer wire-free robot mowers use cameras, LiDAR, or combinations of sensors to navigate even when satellite signals are poor.

How different navigation systems handle trees

No GPS required on some models, but lighting and visual conditions matter

What happens when a mower loses GPS?

Trees can block or reflect satellite signals, especially when they have dense leaves or when the mower operates close to large trunks.

Depending on the mower, it might:

Stop and wait for GPS accuracy to recover.

Switch to camera or other sensor-based navigation.

Lose its precise position and fail to finish mowing an area.

Require manual assistance if it cannot recover its location.

Losing GPS doesn't automatically mean the mower gets physically stuck. However, it can cause interruptions, incomplete coverage, or navigation failures.

What I would buy for a heavily wooded yard

I'd prioritize a LiDAR + camera mower, or a well-tested RTK + visual-navigation hybrid.

A recent real-world comparison by The Verge tested five robotic mowers on a tree-filled, three-quarter-acre property. The Segway Navimow X430 performed particularly well, while the Dreame A3 AWD Pro was a promising LiDAR alternative. 
The Verge

Also, watch out for exposed roots, fallen branches, wet leaves, and uneven ground. These can physically trap a mower even when its navigation works perfectly.

Over 1 acre

Those two details will help determine whether a wire-free mower is likely to work reliably in your yard and which navigation systems are worth considering.

Network RTK, backup systems such as lidar or visual SLAM, and better all-wheel drive helped the machines avoid getting stuck and maintain a lush, consistent lawn.
